Subjective: Pet parent reports that Milo, a 1.4-year-old dog, has started scratching an affected area on his tail. The pet stays mostly indoors and gets grooming approximately once every two weeks. No recent exposure to ticks or outdoor environments except a yard at the hometown. The pet had a tick infestation previously but was treated. The pet parent has noticed mild fever possibly related to recent vaccination.
Objective: Milo weighs approximately 5 kg. The affected area is on the tail with signs consistent with an infection process likely due to excess oil secretion. No other areas of infection noted. Mild fever observed post vaccination. No ticks present currently. Feeding includes a feeder with some treats and commercial food. Water intake appears adequate with use of water fountain.
Assessment: Milo is experiencing a mild skin infection on the tail likely secondary to excess oil secretion (seborrhea) causing itching and scratching. Mild fever is likely a transient reaction to recent yearly vaccination. No evidence of tick infestation currently. Overall health appears stable with appropriate weight and feeding.
Plan: 1. Apply prescribed topical ointment to the affected tail area after gently wiping with pet wipes or a damp cloth. 2. Trim hair around the affected area using a trimmer to allow better ointment application. 3. Monitor for resolution of infection over 2-3 days; if persistent, consider thorough cleaning and re-examination. 4. Administer prescribed oral tablet medication as directed (one tablet for 5 kg body weight). 5. Continue regular grooming every two weeks with slight trimming rather than full shaving. 6. Maintain current feeding regimen with gradual introduction of quality commercial food and treats. 7. Monitor for any new symptoms or worsening condition and report if noted. 8. Follow up as needed for vaccination and parasite control every 3 months.
Conclusion: Milo has a mild skin infection on the tail due to excess oil secretion causing itching and scratching, with mild fever likely related to recent vaccination. Treatment with topical ointment and oral medication along with grooming and monitoring is recommended. No current tick infestation or other systemic issues noted.
DifferentialDiagnosis: 1. Seborrheic dermatitis due to excess oil secretion. 2. Superficial bacterial or yeast skin infection. 3. Allergic dermatitis causing itching and secondary infection. 4. Reaction to vaccination causing mild fever. 5. Parasitic infestation unlikely given no current ticks.
